items.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: my wife Hope wrote a play that’s set in a theater improv workshop. And working with — I not only produced the play but I also played the shows live, with an acoustic guitar.

ctx.x: Even tomorrow night in the concert I noticed they didn’t really bill you as a blank guitarist, which I thought was good. You’re a guitar player and you’re choosing your own program, which sort of brings me to my last question. When you get a song started, it’s a big hall by the way, and you’ve got all those people watching you, and you’ve played the melody, what makes you decide where to go with it?

It depends where I go with an arrangement or a composition. It may be completely set, completely fixed. Even though there’s improvisational arms in there, and even though I may have improvised it in the recording — it’s like Nat King Cole for example — didn’t improvise in concert. He played what he played on the records because that’s what his audiences expected. That’s the entertainer side of the equation. Though it may have been improvised in the studio. So there’s times — I think tomorrow night I’ll probably…
Well this has been fascinating for me, you have encyclopedic knowledge. And as I said I admire the versatility.

items.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Hope, my wife Hope is, other than working with me on the musical that we’re developing

ctx.x: Yeah. Well Laurence I want to thank you for your time and I admire how busy you have remained and your Tea Time with Laurence Juber, and the success.

Yeah, but you know our whole family, I mean Hope, my wife Hope is, other than working with me on the musical that we’re developing, she’s involved in production of a potential TV show. My eldest daughter, Nico, has written a musical, which she did a Zoom reading of last week with a bunch of really high level New York talent. And then my youngest, Ilsey, has become a very successful songwriter. And she is busy writing and hasn’t stopped, you know, learned how to run Pro Tools so she can record vocals at home.…

I’ve got a revenue stream from royalties on thirty albums that I’ve recorded, you know stuff that gets played on Sirius and Pandora, Spotify, and it all kind of keeps things afloat without having the pressure of having to deal with the fact that there’s no money gigs. So, but I miss the live experience obviously.
